tossups.text: The engoma type of this instrument is sometimes used in a therapeutic ceremony called Zebola in the Congo region. The tar is a version of this instrument with a single head played without any tools. The Malinke people play one of these instruments that is goblet-shaped and tuned by thin ropes called the djembe [jem-bay]. An hourglass-shaped version of this instrument played by many different African peoples is known as the "talking" type. For 10 points, skin pulled taut around a wooden head characterizes what common percussion instruments?

The speleologist Anton Suwa died while exploring a cave with this name in Zalog pri Šempetru ("shem-PAY-troo"), located near a gorge with this name outside of Ljubljana. A village with this name in Stjørdal ("stee-YER-dal") takes its name from the Old Norse word for "overhang." Short limestone formations surrounded by shrubbery inspired residents to give this name to a touristy area in West Bay, Grand Cayman. A Michigan town with this name may have been inspired by German travelers shouting the phrase "So beautifully bright!" out of a stagecoach. In 2013, George Kourounis journeyed to the bottom of a location with this name, whose impacts on the local community were addressed by Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow. The Darvaza gas crater in Turkmenistan, which has burned for five decades, is nicknamed the "Door to" this place. Mount Etna was considered a gate to, for 10 points, what location where souls suffer in the afterlife?

This molecule cleaves a double bond into two carbonyls in its namesake "lysis." A scale used for measuring the concentration of this molecule has a baseline of 220 and is named for Dobson. This molecule is depleted in a radical mechanism by chlorofluorocarbons, which caused a "hole" in this substance over Antarctica. For 10 points, name this molecule with formula O3, which forms a layer of the atmosphere responsible for screening UV light.

This poet wrote "let the rose blossom each year" and "Please don't, above all, plant me in your heart" in one collection. In another collection, this author described "the emotion that almost amazes us when a happy thing falls." This author, wrote a poem describing how its title object "glisten[s] like a wild beast's fur." That poem by this author of Sonnets to Orpheus claims "we cannot know his legendary head / with eyes like ripening fruit" while describing the "Archaic Torso of Apollo." A set of 10 poems by this author opens "Who, if I cried out, would hear me among the Angelic orders?" For 10 points, name this German author of the Duino Elegies.

A composer from this country dedicated her Sonata for Harp to Nicanor Zabaleta and wrote "The Knight's Farewell" in memory of another composer from it. A composer from this country taught generations of Americans, including Aaron Copland and Philip Glass. A slow piano piece from this country begins with the left hand playing a low G on beat one, then a higher B minor triad on beat 2. A composer from this country used a saxophone in The Creation of the World and wrote The Ox on the Roof. This country was home to a group of six composers including Darius Milhaud and Francis Poulenc. For 10 points, name this home country of Nadia Boulanger and Erik Satie.

This battle ended when the successor of Syphax, Masinissa, attacked the loser's flank. The losing commander had been isolated following the Battles of Ilipa and the Metaurus River, which saw the losses of Mago and Hasdrubal, and was thwarted by the victor's formation of intentional gaps in their lines between hastati and principe troops, negating the loser's war elephants. Ending a conflict which began with battles at Lake Trasimene and Cannae in Italy, for 10 points, identify this clash in Northern Africa where Scipio Africanus defeated Carthage under Hannibal, winning the Second Punic War for Rome.

One of these works by William Harmon concludes by saying "Whatever happens happens anyway", while other examples of this work describe a certain ability as "not too hard to master" and state that "I learn by going where I have to go". In addition to Elizabeth Bishop's "One Art" and Theodore Roethke's "The Waking", another work in this poetic form calls to "Wild men", "grave men" and "you, my father" to "rage, rage against the dying of the light." For 10 points, name this rhyming 19-line poetic form with five tercets and a quatrain, one of which is Dylan Thomas' "Do Not Go Gentle Into That Good Night".

This event is foreshadowed in a short poem in which a question about weeping maidens who toss sails into the air reveals the identity of the traveller Vegtam. The instigator of this event is killed by a newborn deity who refuses to wash his hands or comb his hair until he does so. During a commemoration of this incident, a bonfire consumes a self-duplicating ring and the goddess Nanna. The mastermind of this event is bound in a cave using the entrails of his son, as poison drips onto his face. Nearly everything in the world is made to promise never to hurt its victim in an attempt to prevent this crime, which Loki orchestrates by deceiving the blind god Hodr. For 10 points, in what event was a beautiful Norse god slain using a spear of mistletoe?

These works title a poem which imagines a goddess from "Northern tales of eld" and asks "Was she made of a milky drop / On the blue of a winter heaven?" Another poem titled for these works likens the sun to a "round, opaque window" which "climbs to the zenith" on "an invalid's steps." The collection Enamels and Cameos includes a poem titled for these works and the color white by Théophile Gautier. Another poem titled for these works describes how the "fiery rays of the Brazilian sun" beat down during a "siesta of the tropics" enjoyed by an "old sea wolf." The speaker describes a cricket and grasshopper playing the violin and guitar and calls the sea a "coarse mirror of silver" in that poem, which Rubén Darío titled for one of these "in Gray Major." For 10 points, name these musical pieces, another of which includes lyrics from an ode about a "daughter of Elysium" written by Friedrich Schiller.

During China's Great Leap forward, Mao ordered that this good be produced in "backyards." Charles M. Schwab turned Bethlehem, Pennsylvania into a major manufacturing center for this good in the 20th century. Along with coal, the earliest ancestor of the EU regulated trade of this good. Pinkerton detectives put down strikers in this industry during the Homestead Strike. For 10 points, Andrew Carnegie made his fortune in the production of this metal, used to build skyscrapers.

Two travelers created by this author eat a group of sentient oysters and "talk of many things," and a singer created by this man sings about "beautiful Soup" after performing at a Lobster Quadrille. A nonsense poem by this man is explained by Humpty Dumpty, and "The Walrus and the Carpenter" is recited by Tweedledee and Tweedledum in this man's Through the Looking-Glass. For 10 points, name this author of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.

One person with this title names an "Assurance" given to Patriarch Sophronius of Jerusalem. Another person of this title rejected a woman's claim to inheriting Fadak. The first holder of this title launched the Ridda Wars to unify his domain. A holder of this title defeated a Byzantine army commanded by Vahan the Armenian in a battle fought near the Yarmouk River. While praying, one holder of this title was killed with a poison-tipped sword wielded by a Kharijite. The First Fitna began after the assassination of one holder of this title, Uthman, who was succeeded by Ali. For 10 points, give this title of four "Rightly-Guided" leaders of Islam.

Elisabeth of Bohemia claimed this book persuaded her of "the nonextendedness of the soul" in a letter to its author, who faced objections from Pierre Gassendi. This work defines clear and distinct ideas in the third of its six sections, the second of which establishes that perception by intellect alone identifies a piece of wax. The narrator of this book wonders if an evil demon is deceiving their senses, prompting them to doubt everything. This book expands on an argument phrased in the author's Discourse on Method as cogito ergo sum, or "I think, therefore I am." For 10 points, name this magnum opus of René Descartes.

During this decade, the exhibit New Documents highlighted the "snapshot-like" photography of Lee Friedlander and Garry Winogrand. In this decade, Vogue began to focus on "Youthquake" culture after Diana Vreeland took over. Square photographs like Identical Twins, Roselle, New Jersey and Child with a Toy Hand Grenade were taken in this decade by Diane Arbus. In this decade, a band put a collage of historical figures and celebrities on one album cover, and then had pop artist Richard Hamilton create a pure white cover for their next album. For 10 points, name this decade in which Richard Avedon photographed the Beatles.

This policy had its origins in the Pass Laws, and several people who were opposed to this policy were sentenced to prison following the Rivonia Trials. The Spear of the Nation was the military wing of a political party which opposed this policy, which led to the Sharpeville Massacre as well as an event in which students who opposed the mandatory teaching of a certain language were fired upon by police, the Soweto Uprising. Ended by F.W. De Klerk and Nelson Mandela, for 10 points, name this policy of racial segregation in South Africa.

Less notable aspects of this document include clauses that men can't be imprisoned because of a female claim unless it's in regards to the death of her husband, and that no town or person could be forced to build a bridge. This document also made it legal for Jews to practice usury, since they were not Christians, they could not be excommunicated for charging interest on loans. This document is perhaps more well known for the implementation of the concepts of habeas corpus and the establishment of a twenty-five baron council to keep the king in check. For 10 points, name this document that greatly curtailed the power of King John, written in 1215.

Ulysses Grant dispatched Horace Capron to establish an agricultural system on this island, the birthplace of Koshamain, which is home to its country's first musical road. The islands of of Rebun and Rishiri lie off the coast of this land mass, while to its North the La Perouse Strait separates it from the Kuril islands, Sakhalin, and the Sea of Okhotsk. Reached from its larger Southern neighbor via the massive Seikan Tunnel across the Tsugaru Strait, for 10 points, name this traditional home of the Ainu people with capital at Sapporo, a Japanese island to the North of Honshu.

Pierre-Ernest Weiss refined a law about these objects concerning behavior above the Curie point, and described a "para" force exerted by some of these objects. A type of these objects can be created by wrapping a wire around a metal core, and can be activated with an electric current. A "ferro" type of these objects'namesake force is displayed by objects of this type made of cobalt, nickel, or iron. For 10 points, name these objects whose "north" and "south" poles can attract each other.

One character in this work preaches the "Salvation and five percent" doctrine and the protagonist helps that character in increasing Sunday school attendance. After giving a speech at the SAREB convention, the protagonist supports the conservative candidate Prout for mayor, but for a short while is affected by the liberal Seneca Doane. When Zilla is shot by her husband Paul Riedling, the protagonist changes his outlook and has an affair with Tanis Judique, but breaks up with her and joins the Good Citizen's League after his wife Myra recovers from illness. For 10 points, identify this novel about a real estate agent from Zenith, a work by Sinclair Lewis.

This region saw the Great Raid of 1840 where Comanches led by Buffalo Hump plundered multiple towns. The Archive War broke out in this region due to disputes over moving its capital to a different city. A new form of currency known as Redbacks was instituted by Mirabeau Lamar, this region's second president. The first flag of this region was known as the "Burnet Flag," which preceded the adoption of a more famous flag that is still in use and that lends its name to a nickname for this region. The Goliad Massacre and the Battle of the Alamo were pivotal moments in this region's revolution. For 10 points, name this short-lived country, known as the Lone Star Republic, that won independence from Mexico at the Battle of San Jacinto and was led by Sam Houston.

parts.text: Identify this portraitist named "First Painter to his Majesty," whose series The Battles of Alexander the Great includes 1673's Alexander and Porus.
Perhaps the best-known work of Charles Le Brun is this part of the Palace of Versailles which he completed alongside the Ambassador's staircase and the Halls of War and Peace.
Le Brun ended up working with this Frenchman in Rome in 1642. This neo-classicist's own works include The Death of Germanicus, Holy Family on the Steps, and Et in Arcadia Ego.

bonuses.leadin: His Death of Meleager earned the respect of Louis XIV. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this state where Caatinga ("ka-ah-CHEEN-ga") landscapes dominate the Chapada Diamantina National Park. This state's second-largest city is Feira de Santana ("FAY-ra jee sun-TAH-na").

The Point of St. Antonio is in this city, which is a center of African-influenced culture home to several mestres of capoeira. The historic Pelourinho ("pay-lo-REEN-yoo") neighborhood is in this capital of Bahia.
Bahia is a state in the eastern part of this country, whose other states include Mato Grosso, Rio Grande do Sul, and Belo Horizonte.

bonuses.leadin: In this state, the Point of St. Antonio lies at the entrance to the Bay of All Saints, which was named for the date in 1501 that Amerigo Vespucci sailed into it. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Carried out by autotrophs such as plants and algae, this process takes light energy from the sun and turns it into chemical energy usable by the cell.
Photosynthesis in eukaryotes takes place in this organelle. Its inside is filled with stroma, while it contains many flat disks called thylakoids.
This enzyme is essential to photosynthesis. Found in the Calvin cycle, it causes carbon fixation by adding carbon dioxide to continue the cycle.

bonuses.leadin: For 10 points each, name the following about an important process in biology.

parts.text: Name this language used by Luís de Camões to write The Lusiads.

This Portuguese poet made a habit of writing using alter egos or "heteronyms" like the pastoral Alberto Caeiro, the Greek-inflected Ricardo Reis, or the Whitmanesque Álvaro de Campos. He also wrote The Book of Disquiet.
Pessoa's diverse influences included this English poet, who described "Water, water everywhere, nor any drop to drink" in The Rime of the Ancient Mariner. He also wrote "Kubla Kahn."

bonuses.leadin: A poem in this language created the mythological character Adamastor. For 10 points each:

parts.text: This artist gained his reputation by working as an engraver under Trumbull. A painting by this artist depicts one of his mentors conversing with William Cullen Bryant on a mountainous peak overlooking a waterfall.

Many of Trumbull's paintings decorate the rotunda of this Washington, DC building, including his depiction of the Declaration of Independence. This building also includes the Apotheosis of Washington and the Frieze of American History.

Many of the most iconic portraits of George Washington were painted by either Trumbull or this other artist, including his Lansdowne Portrait and Athenaeum Portrait, the latter of which appears on the dollar bill.

bonuses.leadin: Answer the following about the "Painter of the Revolution," John Trumbull, for 10 points each.

parts.text: Name this Soviet secret police organization, the predecessor to the KGB. One of its most notorious leaders was Lavrenty Beria.
The NKVD helped carry out Stalin's Great Purge, in which several dissidents were shipped off to these Soviet Labor camps. Solzhenitsyn gave an account of living in one of these.
Joseph Stalin purged this Old Bolshevik and author of The ABCs of Communism. He was a longtime editor of Pravda and fell out of favor for criticizing collectivization.

bonuses.leadin: This organization killed thousands of Polish officers in the Katyn Forest Massacre, and some people believe Sergei Kirov was killed by agents of this organization. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this novel about Offred that is set in the dystopian Republic of Gilead.
The Handmaid's Tale is the most famous novel by this author of The Blind Assassin and Oryx and Crake .
Margaret Atwood is from this country, also home to short story writer and recent Nobel Laureate Alice Munro.

bonuses.leadin: The title character of this novel tries to circumvent the oppressive influence of the Commander and Serena Joy. For 10 points each,

parts.text: In a Somalian legend, humans can partly turn into what animals by rubbing themselves with a stick during the night? Roman geographers presented these real animals as monstrous 'crocotta' that could mimic human speech.

All people with this profession are believed to possess buda and transform into hyenas according to Ethiopian folk tradition. In the Kalevala, the Sampo was created by Ilmarinen, an immortal with this profession.
acceptableAnswers: prompt on inventor with “what other profession did these people have?”

parts.text: Buda is a curse believed to be caused by an "evil" one of these body parts. The wedjat depicts these body parts belonging to Ra and Horus.

bonuses.leadin: People who possess an evil force called buda are able to transform into these animals. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this city whose "Renaissance" was "fathered" by Kenneth Rexroth, who invited Robert Creeley to this city. Allen Ginsberg and Jack Kerouac frequented the City Lights Bookstore in this California city.
Duncan and Creeley taught at this college, whose other poets included Denise Levertov and "projective verse" advocate Charles Olson.
Both Duncan and Creeley were open about the influence of this bisexual Imagist poet of Helen in Egypt. This poet asked the sea to "cover us with your pools of fir" in "Oread."

bonuses.leadin: Donald Allen grouped Robert Duncan, Madeline Gleason, and Jack Spicer under this city's poetic "Renaissance" in the anthology The New American Poetry 1945-1960. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this Roman leader who subdued Vercingetorix during his conquest of Gaul. He later famously crossed the Rubicon and eventually bested Pompey to help establish his short-lived dictatorship.
Julius Caesar made this first Roman emperor his heir. Along with Lepidus and Mark Antony, this man formed the Second Triumvirate before defeating Mark Antony's forces at Actium to secure power.
This man succeeded Augustus as emperor and had earlier conquered Dalmatia, Pannonia, and Germania. As emperor, he withdrew to Capri allowing his advisor Sejanus to rule.

bonuses.leadin: Brutus masterminded this man's assassination on the Ides of March. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Identify this American writer who also penned All My Sons as well as a work in which the titular character kills himself so that his son will get the insurance money to become a successful businessman.
That aforementioned titular character was this salesman, whose decides to kill himself despite reconciling with his son, Biff, in a restaurant.
Arthur Miller also wrote this work, in which Gilres Corey was pressed to death before Proctor, Rebecca Nurse, and Martha Corey were led to the gallows.

bonuses.leadin: He revised his unpopular one-act version of A View from the Bridge to a two-act version, which was more welcomed. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this $4 billion dollar program that rewards states for implementing education reforms.
This woman founded StudentsFirst in order to help reform the education system. This former chancellor of the Washington DC school system also founded The New Teacher Project.
Michelle Rhee is married to Kevin Johnson, the mayor of this capital of California.

bonuses.leadin: Tennessee was awarded more than $500 million during the first round of this national competition, which was announced by the Secretary of Education, Arne Duncan, in 2009. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this work, subtitled "The Birth of the Prison," which describes Bentham's Panopticon and distinguishes between cellular, organic, genetic, and combinatory characteristics of individuality.
acceptableAnswers: Surveiller et punir: Naissance de la Prison

parts.text: This French philosopher wrote Discipline and Punish and discussed the concept of "medical gaze" in his work, The Birth of the Clinic.
This other French philosopher was a proponent of existentialism and wrote Being and Nothingness. He also criticized Foucault's book The Order of Things.

bonuses.leadin: It begins by contrasting the public torture of Robert-François Damiens and a prison in Mettray. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this French-American Dadaist artist who submitted an ordinary porcelain urinal to the Society of Independent Artists, titling it Fountain.
Fountain was one of these types of common, mass-produced items championed by Duchamp as art. These "found objects" also included Bicycle Wheel and Bottle Rack.
Duchamp was an avid fan of this activity, and designed a 6 x 4 [6 by 4] inch "pocket" set of items for this activity. Man Ray created several curvilinear geometric sets of items for this activity.

bonuses.leadin: One of this artist's works was purchased from the J. L. Mott Iron Works store in New York and then signed "R. Mutt 1917." For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this last shogunate [show-gun-ate] of Japan. Commodore Matthew Perry entered Japan while this shogunate was in power.
The Tokugawa shogunate was founded by man, who led it during the Siege of Osaka against the Toyotomi clan. He also led troops during the Battle of Sekigahara.
During the Tokugawa shogunate, this class of noble warriors ranked just under the daimyo in social and political power.

bonuses.leadin: Following the failure of the Shimabara Rebellion during this period, Christians were forced underground. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this country divided by the medieval Principalities of Turov and Polotsk. A rushnyk folk pattern appears on the red, white, and green flag of this country, which historically included Black and White Ruthenia.

Ivan Aksakov called Belarus "West Russia" as part of his "philia" for this group. The brothers Lech, Czech, and Rus are mythic fathers of this ethnolinguistic group, whose "Pan-" movement galvanized Czechoslovak nationalism.

Slavophile movements such as Russia's Pochvennichestvo ("POACH-vyin-yit-shist-vuh") and Ukraine's Ruthenian Triad drew on this "Counter-Enlightenment" philosopher, whose concept of Volksgeist also inspired Germany's Völkisch movement.

bonuses.leadin: Nationalist historians who follow the invalidated Litvinist school credit this modern country's people with founding the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and dub the 16th century its "golden age." For 10 points each:

parts.text: Thunderless "Catatumbo lightning" occurs where its namesake river enters this lake, where it was used as a natural lighthouse for centuries. This lake's western shore has the highest rate of Huntington's disease in the world.
This most lightning-struck country in the world contains the lightning hotspots of Kabare and Kampenem, which are in this country's Lualaba River Basin within a region of cloud forest.
acceptableAnswers: The Democratic Republic of the Congo

parts.text: This state is the "lightning capital" of the U.S. due to the high moisture and sea breezes in its coastal cities, like Tampa. It's also called the "Sunshine State."

bonuses.leadin: Name these "lightning capitals" of the world. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name these images which are self-similar, meaning that any part of the whole magnified, resembles the whole.

One prominent example of a fractal is this fractal named after a Polish mathematician. It can be produced by the Chaos game or by shading in all the odd numbers in Pascal's Triangle. It is recognizable to Legend of Zelda fans as the triforce.
This fractal, named after a French mathematician, is closely related to Julia Set. It is calculated via the escape time algorithm.

bonuses.leadin: Two prominent examples of these types of figures include the Koch Snowflake and the Julia Set. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this author of "Little Red-Cap." This author collected poems about female counterparts to famous male figures such as Charles Darwin and Pontius Pilate in The World's Wife.

In a poem from The World's Wife, this man's widow reflects on being bequeathed his "second best bed." That poem, "Anne Hathaway," is set after this author is buried in his birthplace of Stratford-upon-Avon.

Description acceptable. In a Duffy poem, this person "ages one year in an hour" waiting to celebrate her "Christmas Birthday." A poem addressing this person as a "dear, dear Friend" notes that "five years have past" since a visit to the title place.

bonuses.leadin: In a poem by this author, "poetry" is given as the reason why a character lets a wolf buy her a drink and then kills him with an ax 10 years later. For 10 points each:

parts.text: Name this "people of the longhouse," an alliance of five northeastern Native American tribes who split over the issue of the Revolutionary War. The Great Peacemaker and Hiawatha were instrumental in uniting this people.
The Haudenosaunee fought these conflicts against the French and the Huron to gain control over the fur trade.

It is believed that the laws of the Haudenosaunee served as a basis for this more famous document, which was drafted during namesake conventions and replaced the ineffective Articles of Confederation.

bonuses.leadin: A woman named Jigonhsasee [Jee-cone-sah-say] resolved tribal disputes for this people. For 10 points each:
